title: JOINs: inner, left, right and full

videos.script: Four lessons ago we took a spreadsheet apart into tables. This is the lesson that puts it back together, one question at a time. {{apart}} And there is one sentence that decides whether joins ever feel simple, so here it is before anything else. A join does not merge two tables. It pairs rows. {{pairs}} That sounds like a distinction without a difference until you count. One customer, five orders. Join them and you do not get one row with five orders in it — you get five rows, each carrying a full copy of the customer. {{five}} The customer's name is now written five times in your result. Which is fine, and it is also the source of almost every wrong answer in SQL, because the moment you count those rows, or add up a column, you are counting the customer five times. {{count}} The other half of this lesson is the join where a row has nothing to pair with. A customer who has never ordered. A product never sold. Those rows disappear from an ordinary join, silently, and the question was usually about them. {{missing}} And then the one condition that puts them back and the one place people put it that takes them away again — which is the single most common bug in this entire course, and it does not produce an error. {{bug}}
